# Introduction

Cluster randomized trials (CRTs) randomize intact groups, such as clinics, schools, or geographic areas, rather than individuals, and are the standard design when an intervention is delivered at the group level or when individual randomization would create unacceptable contamination between arms [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. A central assumption underlying standard CRT analysis is the no-interference component of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): a cluster's outcome must not depend on which other clusters were assigned to treatment [@Rubin1986]. This assumption, borrowed from individually randomized trial theory, can fail once clusters are spatially arranged, and so can the weaker assumption of partial interference, under which outcomes may depend on assignments within prespecified groups but not across them [@hudgens_toward_2008]. Tobler's first law of geography, "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" [@tobler_computer_1970], implies that an intervention delivered in one location can plausibly influence outcomes in geographically adjacent locations through shared populations, service networks, information diffusion, or environmental pathways. Documented examples of this kind of spatial spillover span public health and development economics: in a trial of insecticide-treated bed nets in northern Ghana, child mortality was lower in control villages close to treated villages than in control villages farther away [@binka_impact_1998], and a school-based deworming trial in Kenya found health and attendance benefits among untreated children near treated schools [@miguel_worms_2004]. When control clusters benefit from nearby treatment in this way, an unadjusted comparison of treated and control clusters may understate the direct effect, and how much contamination occurs can depend on the spatial arrangement of treated and control clusters, not only on the number of clusters allocated to each arm.

## The design-stage gap in the spatial interference literature

The methodological literature addressing spatial interference in CRTs has concentrated on analysis-stage correction (Chapter 1). Spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ [@moran_interpretation_1948] detect residual spatial dependence once outcomes have been observed, and spatial regression models, such as the spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009] estimated by maximum likelihood [@ord_estimation_1975] and implemented in software [@bivand_r_2022], allow an analyst to separate a direct treatment effect from a spillover effect after the fact. In their systematic review of spatial analysis methods for cluster randomized trials, Jarvis and colleagues placed trials that used spatial separation or buffers outside the primary review of statistical methods [@jarvis_spatial_2017]. The literature therefore offers much more guidance on analyzing spatial effects than on how the choice of treatment assignment itself, made before any data are collected, might reduce the problem.

Design-stage tools do exist, but they were largely developed for a different purpose. Restricted and covariate-constrained randomization address the baseline imbalance that a limited number of clusters can produce [@raab_balance_2001; @moulton_covariatebased_2004]; Crisp and colleagues noted that their extension, which selects clusters from a larger eligible set, also increases spatial dispersion among the selected clusters [@crisp_covariate-constrained_2023]. Their dispersion criterion concerns which clusters are selected rather than how they are assigned to arms, and balancing a covariate across arms does not by itself determine whether treated and control clusters are spatially interspersed in a way that induces contamination. Work that addresses the problem studied here more directly includes randomized saturation designs, which assign different fractions of units treated to different groups so that direct and spillover effects can be jointly identified [@baird_optimal_2018]; the selection of whole clusters for inclusion or exclusion in place of a "fried-egg" design that omits each cluster's outer area from analysis [@mccann_spatial_2018]; and recent theoretical designs under spatial, network and cross-cluster interference and spatio-temporal heterogeneity [@leung_rateoptimal_2022; @cai_independentset_2023; @leung_clusterrandomized_2025; @watson_design_2025]. This chapter complements this work with a simulation comparison of concrete assignment strategies that a trial team could implement, under heterogeneous baseline incidence and a range of spatial dependence and spillover conditions.

## Extending a small-grid proof of concept

Chapter 2 examined block-stratified allocation as a practical way to obtain reasonably good estimation while limiting poor-allocation risk in its studied settings; this chapter evaluates both criteria across a broader set of designs under heterogeneous incidence. We retain its simple random assignment benchmark and strict alternating allocation, called Checkerboard here, while adding incidence balancing, targeting, saturation and isolation strategies. The grid comparison increases the number of clusters from 8--12 to 100, considers queen as well as rook neighbors, and includes heterogeneous baseline incidence in the outcome model. These changes extend the design question rather than provide a direct numerical replication of Chapter 2. In Chapter 2, $\beta$ denotes the intervention effect; here that effect is $\tau$, while $\beta$ denotes the coefficient of the incidence covariate. Our observed-incidence application subsequently uses the North Carolina (NC) community college geography and a continuous education outcome, without assuming that historical sudden unexpected death (SUD) incidence predicts baseline education performance.

## Aims

This chapter has three aims: compare assignment designs by mean squared error (MSE), bias and confidence interval coverage; assess how conclusions depend on incidence heterogeneity, spatial dependence, spillover regime and treatment-effect magnitude; and assess both average accuracy and allocation-specific downside for planning a SUD-prevention education pilot on an observed North Carolina geography. The detailed grid results retain a six-design presentation, with the two related variants documented in the appendix. A main-text benchmark includes all eight strategies and simple random sampling (SRS). The completed application evaluates all nine strategies separately for each observed planning year. The application simulates outcomes and assignments; it does not report outcomes from an implemented intervention.

# Methods

## Spatial structure and outcome model

We simulated a $10\times10$ regular grid of 100 clusters under two definitions of adjacency. Under queen contiguity, two clusters are neighbors if they share an edge or a corner; under rook contiguity, they must share an edge. Queen contiguity is the primary analysis in this chapter. Rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis and the case that continues Chapter 2, whose grids used rook neighbors. For each definition, the binary adjacency matrix was row-standardized to form the spatial weights matrix $W$, so that $WZ$ gives, for each cluster, the proportion of its neighbors that are treated, and $WY$ gives the average outcome among its neighbors. Row-standardization expresses each cluster's spillover exposure as an average over its own neighborhood rather than a raw sum, which would otherwise depend on how many neighbors the cluster has. Within a scenario, the same neighbor type defines $W$ in the outcome model, in the Isolation Buffer design, and in the fitted model.

Cluster-level outcomes $Y$ were generated from a spatial lag model with a spillover term,
\begin{equation}
Y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\left[\tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon\right], \qquad \epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I),
\label{eq:outcome}
\end{equation}
where $Z \in \{0,1\}^{100}$ is the treatment assignment produced by the design under evaluation, $\tau$ is the direct treatment effect of interest, $S(Z)$ is the spillover term defined in Equation \ref{eq:spillover}, $\rho$ is the spatial autoregressive coefficient governing dependence in the outcome beyond that induced by treatment and spillover, $X$ is the baseline incidence covariate with coefficient $\beta = 1$, and $\sigma = 1$. The spatial multiplier $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$ propagates each cluster's shocks through the network of neighbors. We tested $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$. When $\rho = 0$ the multiplier is the identity and the model is a linear regression with independent errors, $Y = \tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon$, in which spatial structure enters only through the spillover term; larger values of $\rho$ induce progressively stronger spatial clustering in the outcome.

We evaluated two spillover regimes,
\begin{equation}
S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \quad \text{(both arms)}, \qquad S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \circ (1 - Z) \quad \text{(control only)},
\label{eq:spillover}
\end{equation}
where $\circ$ denotes the elementwise product. Under the control-only regime, only untreated clusters respond to the treatment status of their neighbors, which represents classical contamination: an untreated cluster's outcome rises with the share of its neighbors that are treated. Under the both-arms regime, every cluster responds to its neighbors' treatment regardless of its own assignment, so neighboring treatment adds to a treated cluster's own effect. We tested four spillover magnitudes, $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, and five magnitudes of the direct effect, $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$, with $\tau = 1$ as the primary scenario throughout.

## Heterogeneous baseline incidence

Chapter 2 assumed a spatially uniform baseline outcome risk. Cluster-level health outcomes typically vary across space, and the designs studied here differ in whether and how they use that variation. We generated the baseline incidence covariate $X$, with values in $(0, 1)$, under three mechanisms. Under the independent (iid) mechanism, each $X_i$ is drawn from a Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution, with no spatial structure. Under the spatially autocorrelated mechanism, $X = \Phi\{(I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u\}$, where $u \sim N(0, I)$, $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function applied elementwise, $W_Q$ is the queen weights matrix, and $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$. Under the Poisson mechanism, a spatially autocorrelated log-rate surface, $\log \lambda = \log(35/100{,}000) + (I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u$ with $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$, generates cluster death counts $C_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i P)$, with an equal population of $P = 100{,}000$ in every cluster, so that a cluster at the base rate expects 35 deaths. The observed rates $C_i / P$ are then rank-normalized to $X_i = (r_i - 0.5)/N$, where $r_i$ is the rank of cluster $i$'s rate among the $N = 100$ clusters and tied rates share their average rank. Ties remain at this population size: the Poisson surfaces used here have between 60 and 76 distinct values among the 100 clusters. The base rate of 35 per 100,000 was chosen to be representative of published SUD incidence: it lies between the SUD incidence rates that Mirzaei and colleagues estimated for US men (49.3 per 100,000) and women (21.7 per 100,000) aged 20--64, close to their average [@mirzaei_years_2019]. It is not the observed rate of the county data described in the Application section, which come from a different source, age range, period, and case definition. The incidence filters always use the queen weights $W_Q$, whichever neighbor type the scenario uses, so the incidence surfaces are identical under rook and queen contiguity. The iid mechanism and the two strengths of each of the other two mechanisms give five incidence configurations.

For each configuration we generated $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, $X_1, \dots, X_{10}$, each from its own seed. The same ten surfaces are used by every scenario in that configuration, across neighbor types, outcome-model parameters, designs, and values of $\tau$; the design draws and the outcome noise are shared more selectively, as described under Simulation design, resampling, and metrics. Each design is applied to the surface that generates the outcome: assignments for surface $k$ are drawn from $X_k$, and the outcome and the fitted model for those assignments use $X_k$ as well. This assumes that the incidence observed when a trial is planned is the incidence that drives its outcome (the matched-surface assumption). The target of each scenario is performance averaged over incidence surfaces; for example, $\text{MSE} = E_X E_{Z \mid X} E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau - \tau)^2]$, with $X$ drawn from the configuration's generator, $Z$ from the design given $X$, and $\epsilon \sim N(0, I)$. Bias, coverage, and power are defined in the same way.

## Treatment assignment designs

We implemented eight treatment assignment designs and present six of them as the primary comparison set in this chapter. The other two, Saturation Quadrants and Balanced Halves, each share the mechanism of a retained design, and in an eight-design comparison at $\tau = 1$ neither could be distinguished from its counterpart under either neighbor type (Appendix \ref{app:eight-design}). Saturation Quadrants assigns the saturations 20\%, 40\%, 60\%, and 80\% to the four quadrants in random order, without reference to incidence; its retained counterpart, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, assigns the higher saturations to the quadrants with higher mean incidence (Table \ref{tab:designs}). We shorten the second name to Incidence-Guided Saturation in the rest of this chapter, as in the figures. Balanced Halves divides clusters into two halves by incidence rank and treats 25 at random in each; its retained counterpart, Balanced Quartiles, uses four strata. In each pair the excluded design had the marginally lower mean squared error or average rank under at least one neighbor type, so the choice of representative does not rest on performance. The two saturation designs performed similarly, so incidence guidance lets a trial direct its highest treatment saturations to the highest-incidence quadrants with little or no loss of estimation accuracy; the accuracy advantage of both designs over SRS, which arises under control-only spillover (see SRS benchmark and allocation-specific risk), comes from the saturation structure they share. Both variants are included in the full benchmark with SRS and in the application.

Table \ref{tab:designs} describes the six retained designs, and Figure \ref{fig:design-samples} shows one assignment from each on a single illustrative incidence surface. Checkerboard is the strict block-stratified allocation of Chapter 2, in which no two rook neighbors share an arm. Chapter 2's Block Stratified Sampling design also admitted relaxed allocations on its $3\times3$ grid, where the arms cannot be balanced; on its $2\times4$ and $3\times4$ grids, as on the $10\times10$ grid here, the strict allocations are the two checkerboard patterns. We use the two names interchangeably for this allocation and use Checkerboard in the rest of this chapter. Checkerboard is the only deterministic design: it gives the same assignment in every draw, although each of its fits still receives its own outcome noise. Every other design was drawn independently 25 times for each incidence surface. Designs that rank clusters by incidence break ties at random, afresh for each draw. High Incidence Focus is random only through that tie-breaking; under the iid and spatial mechanisms incidence values are distinct, so it gives the same assignment in all 25 draws on a surface, and its assignment changes only from one surface to the next. Isolation Buffer builds its assignment from the neighbor type of the scenario, and it treats 38 clusters on average under rook contiguity and 21 under queen contiguity. Every other design treats exactly 50.

## Estimation

We estimated $\tau$ with two maximum likelihood spatial lag models, both fit to every simulated outcome and both including an intercept. The primary, oracle model has the spatial lag $\rho WY$ and the covariates $Z$, $\text{Spill} = S(Z)$, and $X_k$, so it matches the outcome model in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, including the true regime-specific spillover covariate from Equation \ref{eq:spillover}. The oracle model assumes that the analyst knows the form of the spillover mechanism and has the exact exposure term, so its results are a best case for each design; we return to this assumption as a limitation. The non-oracle model, a sensitivity analysis, has the covariates $Z$ and $X_k$ only and omits the spillover term. Both models are fit to the same outcomes.

We fit both models with our own implementation of the maximum likelihood estimator of the spatial lag model [@bivand_comparing_2015], the same estimator that the `lagsarlm` function of the R package `spatialreg` computes with `method = "eigen"`. It maximizes the concentrated log-likelihood over $\rho$, computing the log-determinant from the eigenvalues of $W$ [@ord_estimation_1975], estimates the remaining coefficients by least squares given $\hat\rho$, and computes standard errors from the analytic information matrix. On 5,120 validation fits it agreed with `lagsarlm` to within $9.7\times10^{-8}$ in $\hat\tau$ and to a relative difference of $1.1\times10^{-8}$ in its standard error, at roughly 1\% of the computing time; we also refit a 1\% sample of the full simulation with `lagsarlm` itself as a check. Confidence intervals are 95\% Wald intervals, $\hat\tau \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\text{SE}}$, where $\widehat{\text{SE}}$ is the estimated standard error.

Checkerboard illustrates why interspersion alone cannot guarantee precision. Under rook contiguity on the rectangular grid, $WZ=1-Z$, so treatment and spillover cannot be separately identified; the fitted coefficient on treatment estimates $\tau-\gamma$. Under queen contiguity, treatment is identified but control-only spillover is weakly separated from treatment. We retain Checkerboard in the main design comparison and flag aliased estimates. Exact matrix identities, boundary information and the rare Isolation Buffer aliases are detailed in Appendix \ref{app:technical}. These diagnostics concern the models implemented here.

## Simulation design, resampling, and metrics

The full simulation crossed five values of $\tau$, five incidence configurations, two neighbor types, four values of $\rho$, four values of $\gamma$, two spillover regimes, and eight designs, for $5 \times 5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 8 = 12{,}800$ scenarios, of which the six designs reported in this chapter account for 9,600. We call a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, and spillover regime a block; there are $5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 = 320$ blocks, 160 for each neighbor type. At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, the six designs give 1,920 scenarios, and every block contains all six.

Within each scenario, we drew $J = 25$ assignments from each of the $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, for 250 fits per scenario, and gave every fit its own noise vector, so that fit $(k, j)$ has outcome $Y_{kj} = (I - \rho W)^{-1}[\tau Z_{kj} + S(Z_{kj}) + \beta X_k + \epsilon_{kj}]$; Checkerboard's 250 fits share one assignment but have 250 distinct noise vectors. The ten surfaces are independent, so the surface is the primary sampling unit. Each estimator was fit 3.2 million times. SRS, which assigns exactly 50 of the 100 clusters to treatment by complete randomization, ignoring incidence and geography, was subsequently run with the same matched surfaces, noise keys and 250-fit structure, bringing the complete benchmark to 14,400 scenarios and 3.6 million fits per estimator; the original eight-design results were unchanged.

Every random draw was seeded from a key that names the draw, so the results do not depend on the order in which scenarios are run, and the keys give common random numbers: within a block, all designs share the same noise vectors and incidence surfaces; the five values of $\tau$ reuse the same assignments and noise; and the oracle and non-oracle models are fit to the same outcomes. Blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten surfaces.

For each scenario and estimator, we computed bias, the standard deviation (SD) of $\hat\tau$, MSE, coverage of the 95\% interval, and power, the fraction of fits whose interval lies above zero (a one-sided test of $\tau = 0$ at level 0.025). For both estimators, every one of the 250 fits in every scenario was valid, with a finite estimate and standard error, and the fitting routine raised no warning other than the aliasing flags described above. Because each metric is estimated from a finite number of simulated datasets, it carries simulation (Monte Carlo) error; its Monte Carlo standard error measures this uncertainty and shrinks as more datasets are simulated. Monte Carlo standard errors come from the surface-level metrics: with $m_k$ a metric computed on the 25 fits from surface $k$, $\text{SE}(m) = \text{sd}(m_1, \dots, m_{10})/\sqrt{10}$, and, for metrics pooled over the five incidence configurations, from the 50 independent configuration-by-surface means. Appendix \ref{app:mechanics} gives the parameter grid, the seed keys, and the exact formulas for the metrics, their standard errors, and paired differences between designs.

We compared designs within each neighbor type with a Friedman rank-sum test on scenario MSE [@friedman_use_1937], treating the 160 blocks as repeated measures across the six designs. At $\tau = 1$ we followed it with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons [@nemenyi_distributionfree_1963; @demsar_statistical_2006] and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [@wilcoxon_individual_1945] with Holm's adjustment for multiple comparisons [@holm_simple_1979] for all 15 pairs of designs, and we repeated the Friedman test at each other value of $\tau$. Blocks within an incidence configuration share their surfaces, so these tests treat dependent blocks as independent, which overstates the information about variation from surface to surface. For each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order, we therefore also ran a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over 50 independent units, the 5 configurations times 10 surfaces, with each unit's MSE averaged over that surface's blocks, and a $t_{49}$ interval for the mean difference. Because the values of $\tau$ share assignments and noise, Friedman tests at different values of $\tau$ are not independent confirmations of one another.

We report results separately for each neighbor type, with queen contiguity primary, and no number is averaged over the two. Unless stated otherwise, every number in the Results is pooled over the five incidence configurations, and every table and figure caption states whether it pools the configurations or shows them separately. We report the ranking within each configuration separately and show the split wherever a conclusion changes.

# Results

## Design performance under queen contiguity

At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, under queen contiguity and pooled over the five incidence configurations, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest mean squared error (MSE = 0.091), followed by Balanced Quartiles (0.131), Isolation Buffer (0.160), High Incidence Focus (0.245), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087) (Table \ref{tab:performance}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Coverage of the 95\% intervals was between 0.936 and 0.941 for all six designs (Figure \ref{fig:coverage} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). Power to reject $\tau = 0$ was 0.930 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, 0.827 for Balanced Quartiles, 0.731 for Isolation Buffer, 0.642 for $2\times2$ Blocking, 0.610 for High Incidence Focus, and 0.547 for Checkerboard.

```

The Friedman test rejected equal MSE ranks across the six designs under queen contiguity at $\tau = 1$ ($\chi^2 = 451.57$, $\text{df} = 5$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Nemenyi comparisons (critical difference 0.596) separated 11 of the 15 pairs: Incidence-Guided Saturation ranked significantly better than every other design, including Balanced Quartiles ($p = 0.0086$), Balanced Quartiles ranked significantly better than the remaining four, and the four pairs not separated all lay among the bottom four designs. Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests separated all 15 pairs. Because blocks within an incidence configuration share their ten surfaces, we also compared each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units; every adjacent pair differed significantly (Wilcoxon $p \le 4.9\times10^{-9}$), and the better design had the lower MSE in all 50 units for every pair except High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking (48 of 50). Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons} gives the pairwise results and the critical-difference diagrams.

The bottom three designs were ordered differently by average rank and by mean MSE: by mean MSE, High Incidence Focus (0.245), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087); by average rank, $2\times2$ Blocking (4.24), Checkerboard (4.74), and High Incidence Focus (4.76). Both reversals arise because the MSEs of $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard depended strongly on the spillover regime. Each had a lower MSE than High Incidence Focus in all 80 both-arms blocks (mean MSE 0.062 for each, against 0.162) and a higher MSE in all 80 control-only blocks (0.576 and 2.111, against 0.329). Average rank counts each block once, so their wins under the both-arms regime offset their losses under the control-only regime; mean MSE weights those losses by their size, and the surface-level comparison, which averages each unit over both regimes, also separated High Incidence Focus from $2\times2$ Blocking.

## Design rankings by incidence configuration

Table \ref{tab:by-config} gives each design's MSE within each of the five incidence configurations. Under queen contiguity, the mean-MSE order within every configuration was the same as the pooled order: Incidence-Guided Saturation, Balanced Quartiles, Isolation Buffer, High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking, and Checkerboard. The configuration changed each design's MSE only slightly: in this order, each design's highest MSE across the five configurations was lower than the next design's lowest. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 18 to 21 of the 32 blocks in each configuration. Coverage did not depend on the configuration either: within each configuration, every design's coverage, averaged over its 32 scenarios, was between 0.931 and 0.943. The mechanism that generated the incidence surface therefore did not change the ranking. This includes High Incidence Focus, the design that uses the incidence ranks most directly: its MSE was no higher under the two Poisson configurations than under the iid and spatial configurations.

## Sensitivity to spatial dependence, spillover magnitude, and spillover regime

Under queen contiguity, neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed the ranking. Across $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, no design's MSE changed by more than 0.02. Across $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, the MSE of every design except Checkerboard also varied by less than 0.02, and Checkerboard's varied between 1.052 and 1.108 with no trend in $\gamma$ (Tables \ref{tab:rho} and \ref{tab:gamma} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). Under rook contiguity, $\gamma$ mattered for Checkerboard alone, for the reason given in the rook results below.

The spillover regime was the one factor that changed the queen ranking (Table \ref{tab:regime}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Under the both-arms regime, Balanced Quartiles had the lowest MSE (0.042), followed by Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.046), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.062), Checkerboard (0.062), Isolation Buffer (0.161), and High Incidence Focus (0.162). Under the control-only regime, the order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.135), Isolation Buffer (0.159), Balanced Quartiles (0.219), High Incidence Focus (0.329), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.576), and Checkerboard (2.111); at larger values of $\tau$, Isolation Buffer matched or passed Incidence-Guided Saturation under this regime (see Stability across treatment effect sizes). For Isolation Buffer, no treated cluster has a treated neighbor, so $WZ = 0$ at every treated cluster and $WZ \circ (1 - Z) = WZ$. The two regimes in Equation \ref{eq:spillover} therefore define the same outcome model, and so the same expected MSE; the observed values, 0.161 and 0.159, differ only by Monte Carlo error, because the two regimes use separate draws. Every other design had a higher MSE under the control-only regime, and the increase was largest for Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking, which went from close to the best designs under the both-arms regime to the two worst under the control-only regime. Among the six detailed designs, Incidence-Guided Saturation was first or second under both regimes, at this and every other value of $\tau$, and in the full benchmark that includes SRS (Table \ref{tab:grid-srs}) it remained competitive with SRS under both-arms spillover; this matters because a trial team may not know in advance which regime applies.

The increase under the control-only regime was variance, not bias. The oracle model includes the true regime-specific spillover covariate, so it has no omitted-variable bias. At $\tau = 1$, in every combination of design and regime under queen contiguity, the absolute bias was at most 0.048 and squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was at most 2.2\% of MSE. Checkerboard showed the mechanism most clearly: under the control-only regime its spillover covariate is a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$ at every interior cluster, so only the boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect (Methods). Checkerboard's MSE rose from 0.062 under the both-arms regime to 2.111 under the control-only regime, while its bias stayed near zero (0.004) and its coverage stayed at 0.942: its intervals widened with its variance. Its pooled MSE of 1.087 was almost entirely variance: squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was 0.0045, less than 0.5\% of MSE (Figure \ref{fig:biasvar} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures} shows the decomposition for the Poisson configuration with $\rho_X = 0.20$). $2\times2$ Blocking showed the same pattern on a smaller scale, with MSE rising from 0.062 to 0.576 and a bias of 0.016 under the control-only regime.

## Rook contiguity

Under rook contiguity at $\tau = 1$, pooled over the five incidence configurations, the mean-MSE order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.072), Balanced Quartiles (0.084), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128), Isolation Buffer (0.133), High Incidence Focus (0.206), and Checkerboard (0.480) (Table \ref{tab:performance}; Figure \ref{fig:mse-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}), and the same order held within each of the five incidence configurations (Table \ref{tab:by-config}). Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 97 of the 160 rook blocks (61\%) and Balanced Quartiles in 60 (38\%). Coverage was between 0.938 and 0.942 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was 0.150 (Figure \ref{fig:coverage-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). The Friedman test rejected equal ranks ($\chi^2 = 703.76$, $\text{df} = 5$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer, which were close and traded places at some values of $\tau$; Nemenyi comparisons also left Incidence-Guided Saturation and Balanced Quartiles unseparated, but Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lower MSE in 48 of the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units (Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons}).

Checkerboard under rook contiguity is a different case: $\tau$ is not identified, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$ (Methods). At $\tau = 1$, Checkerboard's mean bias was $-0.502$, $-0.600$, $-0.704$, and $-0.802$ at $\gamma = 0.5$, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8, while its mean standard deviation stayed between 0.20 and 0.21; squared bias, averaged over scenarios, accounted for 0.438 of its MSE of 0.480 (Figure \ref{fig:biasvar-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). Its coverage fell from 0.316 at $\gamma = 0.5$ to 0.027 at $\gamma = 0.8$, and was between 0.134 and 0.161 at every level of $\rho$, against 0.939 to 0.943 under queen contiguity (Table \ref{tab:checkerboard-coverage} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). Because $WZ = 1 - Z$, the two spillover regimes define the same outcome model; the observed MSEs, 0.477 under the both-arms regime and 0.483 under the control-only regime, differ only by Monte Carlo error. Rook Checkerboard estimates were precise but centered on the wrong quantity, the opposite of its imprecise but valid queen estimates. We keep these estimates in every ranking and flag them.

## Non-oracle sensitivity analysis

The non-oracle model, which omits the spillover term, was biased for every design (Table \ref{tab:oracle-nonoracle} in Appendix \ref{app:oracle-nonoracle} gives both models' MSE, bias, and coverage for each design). At $\tau = 1$, and setting aside Checkerboard under rook contiguity, its bias ranged from $-0.12$ to $-0.40$ and its coverage from 0.51 to 0.90 across designs and neighbor types; for Checkerboard under rook contiguity the two models coincide, because once the aliased spillover column is dropped they are the same. Omitting the spillover term also removes a column that can be nearly collinear with $Z$, and the non-oracle estimates were accordingly less variable for some designs. Under queen contiguity, the non-oracle MSE was lower than the oracle MSE for every design, most of all for Checkerboard (oracle 1.087, non-oracle 0.108) and $2\times2$ Blocking (oracle 0.319, non-oracle 0.121); under rook contiguity it was higher for every design except $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128 under both models) and Checkerboard (identical). Where a design's non-oracle MSE was lower, however, its estimate was biased and its intervals under-covered, so the lower MSE does not support valid inference. These results do not change the recommendation: Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest non-oracle MSE under both neighbor types (0.087 under queen contiguity and 0.086 under rook contiguity).

## Stability across treatment effect sizes

Under queen contiguity, each of the two design orders was the same at every $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$: the order by average within-block rank did not change across these values, and neither did the order by mean MSE, although the two orders differ from each other in the bottom three designs (see Design performance under queen contiguity; Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}a shows mean MSE). The Friedman statistic was 455.49, 451.57, 429.01, 411.19, and 376.79 at these five values ($p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$ at each). Under rook contiguity the order was also stable (Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}b) except for the close pair of $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer: by average rank, $2\times2$ Blocking was ahead only at $\tau = 0.8$, and by mean MSE, Isolation Buffer was ahead only at $\tau = 3$. The five values of $\tau$ share their assignments and noise, so these five comparisons are not independent confirmations of one another; they show that, under queen contiguity, the order did not change across the five values of $\tau$ we tested, given the same draws.

Within that stable order, the margins moved. Under queen contiguity, the gap in MSE between Incidence-Guided Saturation and Balanced Quartiles stayed between 0.037 and 0.041, and Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lower MSE of the two in 101 to 103 of the 160 blocks at every value of $\tau$. Isolation Buffer closed the gap instead: its MSE stayed at 0.160 at every value of $\tau$, while that of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.088 to 0.115 and that of Balanced Quartiles from 0.130 to 0.152. Isolation Buffer's gain came under the control-only regime, where the mean MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.131 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\tau = 3$, while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.159 and 0.160. At $\tau = 2$ the two were level (0.1596 for Isolation Buffer against 0.1604), and at $\tau = 3$ Isolation Buffer had the lower control-only MSE (0.160 against 0.182). At $\tau = 2$ and $\tau = 3$, Isolation Buffer also had the lower worst case across all 160 blocks (0.207 against 0.210, and 0.208 against 0.238). Incidence-Guided Saturation remained second under the control-only regime at those two values, second to Balanced Quartiles under the both-arms regime at every value of $\tau$, and lowest in pooled MSE at every value of $\tau$. The rise in its MSE was mostly variance: its mean bias grew from 0.029 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.047 at $\tau = 3$, but squared bias stayed at or below 3.0\% of its MSE. Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes} traces both rises to a term of the estimation error that grows with $\tau$ when treated clusters have treated neighbors, and gives the block-level detail.

Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation kept the lowest control-only MSE at every value of $\tau$, although its margin over Isolation Buffer narrowed, from 0.095 against 0.134 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.131 against 0.136 at $\tau = 3$.

Except for Checkerboard under rook contiguity, coverage stayed close to 0.94 at every value of $\tau$: between 0.936 and 0.941 for every design under queen contiguity, and between 0.937 and 0.942 for every other design under rook contiguity. The coverage of rook Checkerboard, for which $\tau$ is not identified, rose from 0.138 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.442 at $\tau = 3$, because its intervals widened around the wrong quantity (Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes}). Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons} shows coverage across $\tau$ for each design.

## Robustness across blocks

Table \ref{tab:robustness} gives the distribution of MSE across the 160 queen blocks at $\tau = 1$. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest median (0.080) and the lowest worst-case MSE of any design (0.169). Isolation Buffer had the narrowest range (0.128 to 0.206), because its MSE does not depend on the spillover regime, but at a higher level. Balanced Quartiles had a low median (0.115) and a worst case of 0.290. The distributions of $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard reflected their dependence on the spillover regime: both had low first quartiles (0.062 and 0.063) and high upper quartiles (0.580 and 2.093). Checkerboard had the highest MSE in all 80 control-only blocks; in the 80 both-arms blocks, the highest MSE belonged to High Incidence Focus in 42 and to Isolation Buffer in 38. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest worst-case MSE (0.138). These worst cases summarize variation across parameter settings; they are distinct from the conditional risk across assignments within one setting, examined next.

## SRS benchmark and allocation-specific risk

At $\tau=1$ under queen contiguity, pooled over the five incidence configurations and all spatial/spillover settings, Incidence-Guided Saturation has mean MSE 0.0907 against SRS 0.1285; Saturation Quadrants has 0.0900. Table \ref{tab:grid-srs} separates the regimes and includes all eight strategies, and Figure \ref{fig:grid-srs} shows the six detailed designs and SRS with the five incidence configurations kept separate: within each regime the configurations lie close together for every design, whereas the regime changes how each design compares with SRS. Incidence-Guided Saturation's control-only ratio to SRS is 0.631, whereas its both-arms ratio is 1.083. SRS, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves have similar both-arms accuracy. Small mean differences should not be interpreted as equivalence, nor should pooling the regimes obscure the difference in design guidance. Paired comparisons over 50 independent configuration-by-surface units support the lower pooled MSE of both saturation designs relative to SRS; the six-design Friedman rankings elsewhere describe that subset only.

To assess allocation risk, we additionally conducted a focused grid pilot with queen weights, $\tau=1$, two fixed surfaces from each incidence configuration and the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$, $\rho\in\{0,0.5\}$ and $\gamma\in\{0.5,0.8\}$. For assignment $a$, its risk is the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau-\tau)^2\mid a,X]$. We estimated it by simulating repeated outcomes for each sampled assignment and then compared its distribution across assignments. This is different from the distribution of squared errors in a single allocation or MSE across parameter scenarios. The pilot used 100 assignment draws for each randomized design and 100 simulated outcomes per distinct assignment, and selected settings were refined to 400 outcomes on the same assignments; a design with only one possible assignment received its own outcome replication.

Averaged over the 40 units per regime in the pilot (fixed surfaces crossed with the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$), Incidence-Guided Saturation's control-only mean MSE is 0.1409 against SRS 0.2172, the estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE is 0.1747 against 0.2980, and the estimated worst-decile mean is 0.1936 against 0.3486. Under both arms, the corresponding mean MSE is 0.0458 against 0.0428 and worst-decile mean 0.0582 against 0.0544. Saturation Quadrants also performs favorably under control-only spillover; Table \ref{tab:downside} in the application section compares every design with SRS on both criteria. These selected-unit results support a qualified downside argument for saturation; they are not the full-study grid estimates. The focused refinement preserves the control-only direction but reveals substantial outcome-noise contributions to estimated allocation variation, especially under both arms. Quantiles and worst-decile membership estimated from a finite number of outcomes remain uncertain. We therefore use the completed NC application below as the next setting-specific assessment rather than extrapolate exact tail protection from this pilot.

# Application: Observed NC SUD Incidence for Education-Pilot Planning

## Purpose and observed inputs

The application asks which allocation designs estimate a known education-intervention effect accurately on this geography, when some designs use historical SUD incidence to direct treatment. It supports planning an education intervention for healthcare professionals involved in SUD prevention. There are no observed intervention outcomes and no estimated relationship between local SUD incidence and education ability. Any eventual effect on SUD incidence requires a separate clinical evaluation. A real pilot might realize only one allocation per planning year, making both average estimation error and poor-allocation downside relevant.

The assignment units are 58 community college service-area clusters that partition North Carolina's 100 counties under the study mapping (Figure \ref{fig:service-areas}). Northampton is assigned to Halifax Community College, Bertie to Martin Community College, and Hertford alone to Roanoke-Chowan Community College; these are analysis conventions, not exclusive service commitments. Observed county-year deaths and population estimates for ages 18--64 from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program were aggregated to the same named clusters for each year, 2018--2021. SUD deaths were identified from death certificates with the case-adjudication algorithm of Gan and colleagues [@gan_factors_2019]. The corrected numerator supplied by Habib includes heart-failure deaths formerly excluded as presumed non-sudden (A. Habib, personal communication, September 25, 2026). It totals 23,523 deaths over 25,594,321 person-years. The earlier numerator reproduces the totals behind Habib's unpublished report [@habib_temporal_2026]; the corrected numerator is the application input. We do not infer undocumented upstream exclusion rules or zip-code allocation from the received county panel.

Annual incidence is $100,000D_{iy}/P_{iy}$, and pooled incidence is $100,000\sum_yD_{iy}/\sum_yP_{iy}$, with the latter population sum interpreted as person-years. All 58 clusters are present in each year, and counts and populations sum back to statewide totals. We hold these observed annual surfaces fixed, generate no synthetic incidence surface and report years separately (Figure \ref{fig:nc-observed}). The county death-certificate source data are restricted and not publicly available; only 58-cluster summaries are reported. The data were obtained under University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Institutional Review Board protocol 14-2036, "Sudden Unexpected Death in North Carolina" (principal investigator Ross J. Simpson, Jr., Department of Medicine).

## Geographic adaptations and treatment budgets

Queen contiguity between service areas, computed from legal county boundaries, defines primary adjacency, and rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis. Shared legal boundaries across water can create adjacency; this is a prespecified geographic exposure proxy, not a measured professional communication network.

All eight designs and SRS are evaluated under the names used on the grid, adapted to the irregular map; Appendix \ref{app:nc} gives the rules in full and maps the fixed regions and example assignments. Checkerboard becomes a deterministic greedy graph-coloring assignment, an interspersion analog rather than a literal rectangular checkerboard or an exact bipartite coloring. High Incidence Focus treats the 29 highest annual-rate clusters, Isolation Buffer draws a greedy random maximal independent set on the NC adjacency graph, SRS treats a random 29 of 58 clusters, and Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves stratify annual rate ranks and treat 29 overall. The two saturation designs use one fixed four-region partition for all years, chosen for geographic compactness and balance without consulting outcomes. Saturation Quadrants randomly assigns 20/40/60/80\% to these regions each draw; Incidence-Guided Saturation ranks the regions by the mean rank of their clusters' annual per-capita rates and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest; mean raw rates and pooled regional rates serve as prespecified alternative regional summaries. On the NC map, $2\times2$ Blocking uses spatial blocks of nearby clusters, 14 irregular groups formed once per year, and treats half of each group, rounded, at random. Treatment budgets (numbers of treated clusters) therefore differ across designs; we report them rather than modify the designs to force equal budgets (Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets}).

## Outcome model and Monte Carlo evaluation

For the primary education outcome, we set $\beta=0$ in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, use the 58-cluster $W$, and fix $\tau=1$, $\sigma=1$:
\begin{equation}
Y=(I-\rho W)^{-1}[\tau Z+S(Z)+\epsilon],\qquad \epsilon\sim N(0,I).
\label{eq:nc-education}
\end{equation}
Observed incidence affects assignments but neither baseline education nor the constant structural intervention effect. We estimate $\tau$ with the same validated maximum likelihood implementation as in the grid study, with an intercept, $Z$ and the true regime-specific $S(Z)$, without $X$. As in the grid model, $\tau$ is the coefficient before spatial propagation, not an average total impact after applying $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$.

Primary queen settings cross $\rho=0,0.2,0.5$, $\gamma=0.5,0.8$, both regimes, four years and nine designs (432 reported settings). A matched hypothetical baseline sensitivity adds $X=(\operatorname{rank}_{\rm average}(rate)-0.5)/58$ with $\beta=1$ to both the outcome baseline and the fitted covariates (432 settings). It changes baseline and adjustment together and is not an empirical incidence--education association. A rook-contiguity sensitivity analysis of the primary model uses the extreme values $\rho=0,0.5$ (288 settings), and the two alternative regional summaries add 96 Incidence-Guided Saturation settings. The full application reports 1,248 settings, computed from 936 distinct simulation settings, because reported settings with the same allocations and outcome model share one simulation.

We sampled $J=100$ assignments and simulated $R=100$ independent outcomes per distinct assignment; a design whose set of possible assignments contains only one assignment instead received $R=1,000$ outcomes for that assignment, rather than 100 repeated copies of it counted as separate allocations. A prespecified adaptive schedule extended allocations or outcomes where needed until the Monte Carlo standard error of mean MSE was at most 5\% of mean MSE and that of coverage at most 0.01; two single-assignment settings in the matched sensitivity analysis required $R=2,000$, and all randomized designs met these targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$ (Appendix \ref{app:nc}). In the primary model, Checkerboard, Saturation Quadrants, Isolation Buffer and SRS reuse the same simulations across years, because annual incidence enters neither their allocation nor the outcome model. These repeated values are not independent annual confirmation.

For each allocation $a$, the repeated outcomes estimate the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau-\tau)^2\mid a,\text{observed inputs}]$, the expected squared error of the estimate if $a$ were the allocation realized. We report its distribution across sampled allocations, its estimated 90th percentile and the estimated mean among the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, alongside unconditional mean MSE, bias and coverage. A separate tail refinement at queen $\rho=0,0.5$, $\gamma=0.8$, both regimes and all years and designs kept the same allocations and extended the randomized designs to $R=400$ outcomes per allocation, keeping $R=1,000$ for single-assignment designs; it is not a new allocation sample. Worst-decile assignments were identified with one half of the simulated outcomes and evaluated with the other half, to avoid selection bias. Design-matrix rank, residual treatment information, aliased columns, warnings, invalid estimates or intervals, and boundary estimates of $\rho$ were recorded.

## Completed results: accuracy, inference and reach

The main run generated 7,598,000 independent outcome fits. Every setting is complete and meets its prespecified precision targets for mean MSE and coverage: the largest relative Monte Carlo standard error of mean MSE is 0.04871 and the largest Monte Carlo standard error of coverage is 0.00892. There are no warnings, aliased columns, estimates of $\rho$ at the boundary of its parameter space or estimation failures. The tail refinement adds 2,280,000 independent outcomes; counting the outcomes reused from the main run only once gives 9,878,000 distinct outcomes across the two stages. Monte Carlo precision describes uncertainty in simulated performance; it does not certify interval calibration.

Figure \ref{fig:nc-mse} compares the eight designs with SRS by year and regime. Under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants has descriptive mean MSE 0.22329 against SRS 0.30761, a 27.4\% reduction. Incidence-Guided Saturation reduces mean MSE by 21.1--29.9\% across the four observed years (Table \ref{tab:nc-year}). Both saturation designs have lower mean MSE than SRS in every primary parameter setting, and approximate Monte Carlo intervals for each setting-specific difference excluded zero. Neither is uniquely best: as on the grid, the two performed similarly, and their advantage over SRS comes from the saturation structure both designs share. High Incidence Focus is year-sensitive under control-only spillover and cannot be recommended uniformly.

Under both-arms spillover, SRS mean MSE is 0.07638, Saturation Quadrants 0.07518, and Incidence-Guided Saturation ranges from 0.07428 to 0.07682 across years. SRS remains competitive with balancing, blocking and saturation. Small point differences do not establish equivalence or universal optimality. High Incidence Focus has low both-arms MSE in the primary model, but its allocation is deterministic for these fixed rates; this is conditional model-based accuracy, not evidence of randomization-based causal validity.

Mean annual coverage across primary settings is approximately 92.6--93.6\%, below nominal 95\%. The full year/design/regime bias and coverage table is in Appendix \ref{app:nc}. Meeting the Monte Carlo precision targets does not repair this finite-sample undercoverage. Checkerboard's treatment effect is identified on this irregular graph, but weak treatment--spillover separation makes its estimates imprecise; this differs from exact rook non-identification on the rectangular grid.

Population shares contextualize performance (Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets}). High Incidence Focus treats 29 clusters but only about 22--24\% of working-age population, while Isolation Buffer treats a mean of 15.89 clusters and about 27\%. These population denominators measure geographic reach, not the number of healthcare professionals educated, intervention cost or participant-level precision.

## Allocation downside and sensitivity

At the two refined queen settings, $\rho=0$ and $\rho=0.5$ with $\gamma=0.8$, under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants's estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE is 31.8--32.9\% below SRS and its estimated worst-decile mean 34.6--37.8\% below. Incidence-Guided Saturation's corresponding reductions are 20.8--38.6\% and 20.7--43.4\%. The pattern persists under the split-half evaluation described above. Figure \ref{fig:nc-risk} in Appendix \ref{app:nc} shows the $\rho=0.5$ setting. This supports a descriptive downside benefit alongside lower average error, conditional on the studied model and sampled assignments.

Table \ref{tab:downside} compares every design with SRS on both criteria, mean conditional MSE and the mean of the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, in the grid pilot and at the refined NC settings. Under control-only spillover, both saturation designs had lower mean and worst-decile MSE than SRS in both settings. Isolation Buffer also had a lower worst decile than SRS under control-only spillover (0.62 of SRS in the grid pilot and 0.91 in NC), but under both-arms spillover its mean was 3.79 and 3.69 times that of SRS, and it treated fewer clusters. High Incidence Focus has a single allocation in NC. That allocation's MSE was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes (0.76 under both arms and 0.64 under control-only spillover), with mean MSE close to SRS (0.93 and 1.03). In the grid pilot, however, its both-arms mean was 3.91 times that of SRS, and its NC result depends on the incidence model (next paragraph). Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves matched SRS on both criteria. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion in any setting.

Tail uncertainty remains material. With $J=100$, the worst decile contains only ten sampled draws; extra outcomes reduce noise in $\hat m(a)$ but do not enlarge the allocation sample. All 112 reported settings in the tail refinement for designs with more than one possible assignment flag uncertain worst-decile membership. Under both arms, the overlap between the worst deciles identified by the two outcome halves (the Jaccard index: allocations in both divided by allocations in either) was 0--0.25 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, and approximately 61--86\% of the raw variance of estimated risk across allocations was attributable to outcome Monte Carlo noise. Saturation Quadrants's worst-decile membership was similarly unstable. Small both-arms tail differences therefore do not establish superior downside protection. Checkerboard and High Incidence Focus each have only one possible assignment for these inputs; their 90th percentile and worst-decile mean equal their conditional mean MSE, which does not imply low error or absence of outcome uncertainty.


In the matched hypothetical incidence-baseline/X-adjusted sensitivity, High Incidence Focus MSE rises to roughly 3.68--4.44 times its primary value under both arms and 1.42--2.52 times under control-only spillover. Treatment--incidence alignment leaves less residual treatment information after adjustment; this sensitivity changes baseline and adjustment jointly and does not imply that SUD incidence predicts education ability. Rook and queen comparisons matched at the same extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$ preserve broad regime-specific conclusions. Alternative regional summaries change the regional ordering in some years; where an alternative summary gives the same ordering and ties, it gives the same set of possible assignments and so the same results. We retain the prespecified mean-rank rule rather than select a summary retrospectively. Appendix \ref{app:nc} reports the matched sensitivity table and regional ordering.

The application supports considering either saturation strategy when control-only spillover is plausible, and SRS alongside other randomized strategies when both-arm exposure is expected. A trial team should consider likely spillover, recruitment, cluster and participant budgets, achievable measurement precision and interval calibration before selecting one realized allocation. The findings do not establish intervention effectiveness or a final trial protocol.

# Discussion

## Summary and relevance

We compared six treatment assignment designs in the detailed grid ranking, plus two related variants and SRS, for a spatial cluster randomized trial on a grid of 100 clusters, under three mechanisms of heterogeneous baseline incidence, two spillover regimes, and a range of values for spatial dependence, spillover magnitude, and the treatment effect. Some findings held across the incidence configurations and the values of $\rho$, $\gamma$, and $\tau$ under queen contiguity. Others depended on the spillover regime, which a trial team may not know in advance.

We judged each design on two criteria: its average MSE, and the spread of MSE across the allocations it can produce. A trial realizes one allocation, so a design with a low average MSE can still give a poor estimate if some of its allocations perform badly. Chapter 2 compared simple random and block stratified sampling on the same two criteria. The spread matters most for SRS under control-only spillover: in the grid pilot, the worst 10\% of SRS allocations had mean conditional MSE 0.3486, against 0.2172 for SRS allocations overall.

Under queen contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest mean squared error (0.091) and Balanced Quartiles the second lowest (0.131), and the same two designs led under rook contiguity (0.072 and 0.084). Under queen contiguity, the order of the six designs was the same in each of the five incidence configurations and at every value of $\tau$, and neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed it; the mechanism that generated the incidence surface changed each design's MSE modestly (by under 10\%, except High Incidence Focus). Coverage of the 95\% intervals was close to 0.94 for every design under both neighbor types, except Checkerboard under rook contiguity, so the designs differed in precision and coverage did not separate them.

The spillover regime was the one factor that changed the queen ranking. Under queen contiguity at $\tau = 1$, Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking were close to the best designs when spillover reached both arms and were the two worst when it reached only control clusters (MSE 0.062 and 2.111 for Checkerboard, 0.062 and 0.576 for $2\times2$ Blocking), and Balanced Quartiles also lost ground under the control-only regime (0.042 and 0.219), while Incidence-Guided Saturation was first or second among the six detailed designs under both regimes at every value of $\tau$ and remained competitive with SRS under both-arms spillover. Its control-only MSE did rise with $\tau$, and Isolation Buffer, whose MSE did not, matched it under that regime at $\tau = 2$ and passed it at $\tau = 3$. A design whose performance depends on the regime carries a risk that its average MSE does not show.

Checkerboard, the strict allocation of Chapter 2, failed for different reasons under the two neighbor types. Under queen contiguity its estimates stayed centered on $\tau$ with close to nominal coverage but were imprecise, because under the control-only regime only the boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect; under rook contiguity $\tau$ is not identified, and its estimates were centered on $\tau - \gamma$. Checkerboard intersperses treated and control clusters as finely as the grid allows, and both failures come from the dependence this pattern creates between $Z$ and the spillover covariate (Methods).

Together, the grid benchmark, the allocation-risk results (Table \ref{tab:downside}) and the NC application give guidance by scenario. When spillover is expected to reach mainly control clusters, Incidence-Guided Saturation and Saturation Quadrants had the lowest mean MSE and among the lowest worst-decile MSE, so they are the designs we recommend over SRS. Isolation Buffer also limited downside in that regime, but it should be considered only when both-arms spillover is implausible and a smaller treated budget is acceptable. When spillover is expected to reach both arms, the spread of MSE across allocations was small for SRS and the balancing and saturation designs, and SRS, Balanced Quartiles, Balanced Halves and the saturation designs performed about equally, so SRS remains a reasonable choice. High Incidence Focus gave one fixed allocation whose MSE in NC was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes. Its accuracy is model-based rather than randomization-based, however: it was about four times worse than SRS under both arms in the grid pilot, and its MSE rose 1.4--4.4-fold when baseline outcomes were related to incidence. It is a candidate only when historical incidence can be assumed unrelated to the outcome. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion. The NC model assesses education outcomes rather than assuming that historical SUD incidence predicts education ability or a heterogeneous intervention effect.

Saturation Quadrants, which assigns the same saturations without reference to incidence, performed similarly to Incidence-Guided Saturation (see Treatment assignment designs), so their accuracy advantage over SRS under control-only spillover comes from the shared saturation structure, and incidence guidance lets a trial direct its highest treatment saturations to the highest-incidence regions with little or no loss of estimation accuracy.

These are design-stage results, and they complement analysis-stage modeling rather than replace it. Every design was analyzed with a spatial lag model that included the spillover term, and, in the grid study, for every design whose $\tau$ was identified the estimates were close to unbiased: at $\tau = 1$, the absolute bias of each design under each regime was at most 0.048 under queen contiguity and 0.027 under rook contiguity. Given that model, the choice of design determined how precisely $\tau$ was estimated.

## Relation to Chapter 2

Chapter 2's practical argument considered reasonably good estimation together with protection against poor allocation in its studied small-grid settings. We preserve both criteria while extending the designs, geography and incidence conditions. Our findings concern these new models and settings; they do not directly compare numerical results across chapters. The rectangular Checkerboard and its graph adaptation illustrate why a restricted allocation's low assignment variation must be interpreted together with its level of estimation error. The application also separates incidence-guided assignment from assumptions about education outcomes. No direct cross-chapter result comparison is needed to motivate these extensions.

## Limitations

These conclusions have several limitations. First, the primary estimator is an oracle. It includes the exact spillover exposure term, so its results are a best case for each design. We fit a non-oracle model that omits the spillover term as a sensitivity analysis; it was biased for every design and its intervals under-covered, but Incidence-Guided Saturation still had the lowest MSE under both neighbor types. The non-oracle model is only one departure from the oracle. We did not study an analyst who includes a spillover term of the wrong form, such as one built on the wrong neighbor definition or a distance decay.

Second, in the synthetic grid study, the designs and the fitted model used the incidence surface that generated the outcome (the matched-surface assumption in Methods). In practice, planning incidence is estimated from an earlier period and measured with error. The designs that assign treatment by incidence rank, and the covariate adjustment, would then use a noisy surface, and we did not study how that changes the comparison.

Third, in the Poisson mechanism every cluster had the same population of 100,000. Real clusters, including the community college service areas in the Application, differ in population, so their observed rates differ in precision, and unequal populations may change how the designs that use incidence perform.

Fourth, the full synthetic comparison uses one regular $10\times10$ grid, with $\beta$ and $\sigma$ fixed at 1. The application adds one irregular 58-cluster geography and unequal observed populations, but does not constitute a systematic sweep over graph sizes, structures or participant budgets. Some grid results depend on its boundary geometry, while application design adaptations also change assignment support.

Fifth, the simulation shares random draws by design. Blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten incidence surfaces, so the block-level tests treat dependent blocks as independent, which is why we also compared adjacent designs over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. The five values of $\tau$ also share their draws, so the stability of the design order across $\tau$ is not an independent replication at each value (see Stability across treatment effect sizes).

Sixth, the simulation's base rate of 35 per 100,000 is not the rate of the county data described in the Application (see Heterogeneous baseline incidence); we kept it deliberately, because the simulation is a general design study rather than a calibration to one data set. In the Poisson mechanism, incidence enters the designs and the fitted model only through the ranks of the observed rates, so the base rate affects the simulation only through the spatial pattern of those ranks and the number of tied rates.

Seventh, application results are conditional on a continuous education-outcome model with known spillover form and constant structural effect, not an observed education intervention or demonstrated reduction in SUD. Working-age population is a geographic denominator rather than a sample of healthcare professionals. Historical rates are held fixed, so uncertainty in their measurement and changes between planning and implementation are not propagated. The matched baseline sensitivity is hypothetical.

Eighth, 95\% Wald coverage remains below nominal in both the identified grid settings and the application. Greater Monte Carlo precision does not repair this calibration. The finite-outcome allocation-tail estimates do not remove noise from individual risks or establish population worst cases. Settings and years that share the same simulations cannot be treated as independent confirmation. Budgets also differ; these are evaluations of retained strategies, not an equal-cost optimization.

## Future work

The next trial-design steps are to specify the education endpoint, eligible professionals, implementation budget and plausible spillover network, then assess interval calibration for that protocol before randomization. Additional methodological work could study noisy planning incidence, effect heterogeneity, misspecified exposure networks, unequal participant precision and a broader set of graph geometries. A larger allocation sample could sharpen downside estimates if that precision is needed for a final choice. These are extensions of the completed application, not missing analyses required to characterize the prespecified settings reported here.

Each excluded design was compared with its retained counterpart by the Nemenyi and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests described under Simulation design, resampling, and metrics, applied here to all eight designs. Saturation Quadrants's mean squared error was 0.0900, against 0.0907 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, under queen contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 0.98$; Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank $p = 0.41$), and 0.0708 against 0.0717 under rook contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.82$). Saturation Quadrants had the marginally lower mean under both neighbor types and the better average rank in the eight-design comparison (2.100 against 2.350 under queen contiguity and 2.281 against 2.306 under rook contiguity), so retaining Incidence-Guided Saturation as the representative of the saturation mechanism does not rest on performance. Balanced Halves had a mean squared error of 0.1299, against 0.1308 for Balanced Quartiles, under queen contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.88$), and 0.0842 against 0.0837 under rook contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.82$). The two designs differ only in how finely they stratify on incidence, and we retain the finer, four-stratum version. Balanced Halves had the marginally lower mean and the better average rank under queen contiguity (3.312 against 3.356), and Balanced Quartiles had both under rook contiguity (2.919 against 3.038). Under both neighbor types, each excluded design is adjacent to its retained counterpart in mean MSE (Table \ref{tab:eight-design}). The MSEs and coverages of the six retained designs are those of Table \ref{tab:performance}, given here to four and three decimal places.

## A2. Simulation mechanics

\applabel{A2}{app:mechanics}This section gives the mechanical details behind Simulation design, resampling, and metrics (Methods): the parameter grid, the random-number streams, the Monte Carlo structure, and the exact formulas for the metrics and their Monte Carlo standard errors.

**Parameter grid.** Table \ref{tab:parameter-grid} lists the parameters that were crossed to form the 12,800 scenarios and the settings that were held fixed.

\label{tab:parameter-grid}

Incidence configuration & iid; spatially autocorrelated, $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$; Poisson, $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$ & 5 \\
Neighbor type & Queen (primary), rook (sensitivity) & 2 \\
Outcome spatial dependence $\rho$ & 0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50 & 4 \\
Spillover magnitude $\gamma$ & 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 & 4 \\
Spillover regime & Both arms, control only (Equation \ref{eq:spillover}) & 2 \\

Assignments per surface & $J = 25$ (Checkerboard: one assignment, used in every draw) & \\

Estimators & Oracle (primary) and non-oracle (sensitivity), both fit to every simulated outcome & \\

\bottomrule

\end{tabular}

\end{table}
```

**Random-number streams.** Every random draw in the simulation has its own seed, computed by hashing a key that names the draw. The key lists the draw's type (incidence surface, assignments, or noise) and the parameters that identify it, with numeric values written to a fixed number of decimal places so that equal values always give the same key. The random-number generator and its methods for normal and discrete draws are also fixed explicitly, so the streams do not depend on software defaults. Table \ref{tab:seed-keys} lists the three kinds of draw, the parameters in their keys, and the scenarios that therefore share them. The consequences of this scheme, independence from the order of execution and common random numbers, are described in Methods.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[!htb]

\small
\centering

\caption{Seed keys. Each key names the kind of draw and the parameters listed here; the incidence mechanism is iid, spatial, or Poisson, and the iid configuration, which has no $\rho_X$, uses 0 in its place. $k$ indexes the incidence surface and $d$ the design. A draw is shared by every scenario whose key parameters match its own.}
\label{tab:seed-keys}

\begin{tabular}{p{4.2cm}p{5.0cm}p{5.2cm}}

\toprule
Draw & Key parameters & Shared by \\

\midrule
Incidence surface $X_k$ & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, $k$ & Every block, design, and value of $\tau$ of the configuration \\
The $J = 25$ assignments of design $d$ on surface $k$ & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, spillover regime, $k$, $d$ & All five values of $\tau$ and both estimators \\
The 250 noise vectors of a block & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, spillover regime & All eight designs, all five values of $\tau$, and both estimators \\

\bottomrule

\end{tabular}

\end{table}
```

**Monte Carlo structure and checkpoints.** Within a scenario, fit $(k, j)$, with $k = 1, \dots, 10$ and $j = 1, \dots, 25$, uses surface $X_k$, assignment $Z_{kj}$, and noise vector $\epsilon_{kj}$, the $(k, j)$ column of the block's $100 \times 250$ noise matrix (see Simulation design, resampling, and metrics). The unit of computation is a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, and $\rho$: 40 units, each covering 4 values of $\gamma$, 2 spillover regimes, 8 designs, 5 values of $\tau$, 250 fits, and 2 estimators. The units ran in parallel, and the run stops if any unit fails. Each unit's results are saved together with a record of the parameter settings, the simulation code, and the software versions that produced them, and saved results are reused only if all of these match the current run, so results from different code or settings are never combined.

**Scenario metrics.** For one scenario and estimator, let $f = 1, \dots, n$ index the valid fits, those with a finite estimate and standard error (here every fit was valid, so $n = 250$). Let $L_f, U_f = \hat\tau_f \mp z_{0.975}\,\widehat{\text{SE}}_f$, where $z_{0.975} = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) \approx 1.96$, and let $\bar{\hat\tau} = n^{-1}\sum_f \hat\tau_f$. Then
$$
\text{Bias} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\tau_f - \tau), \qquad
\text{SD} = \left\{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\left(\hat\tau_f - \bar{\hat\tau}\right)^2\right\}^{1/2}, \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\tau_f - \tau)^2,
$$
$$
\text{Coverage} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{L_f \le \tau \le U_f\}, \qquad
\text{Power} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{L_f > 0\},
$$
so that $\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + (n-1)\,\text{SD}^2/n$.

**Surface-level standard errors.** For $m \in \{\text{Bias}, \text{MSE}, \text{Coverage}, \text{Power}\}$, let $m_k$ be the same formula applied to the valid fits from surface $k$ (here all 25). With $K = 10$ and $s(a_1, \dots, a_K) = \{(K-1)^{-1}\sum_k (a_k - \bar a)^2\}^{1/2}$ the sample standard deviation,
$$
\text{SE}(m) = \frac{s(m_1, \dots, m_K)}{\sqrt{K}}, \qquad m \pm t_{0.975,\,K-1}\,\text{SE}(m).
$$
Because every fit was valid, each surface contributes 25 fits and $m = K^{-1}\sum_k m_k$. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ in the same block at the same $\tau$, the difference is paired at the surface level: with $\Delta_k = m_{d,k} - m_{d',k}$,
$$
\text{SE}(m_d - m_{d'}) = \frac{s(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_K)}{\sqrt{K}},
$$
with the same $t_{0.975,\,K-1}$ interval.

**Standard errors pooled over configurations.** For one design, neighbor type, and value of $\tau$, let $\mathcal{B}_c$ be the 32 blocks of configuration $c$ and $m_{b,k}$ the surface-$k$ metric in block $b$. The configuration-by-surface means and the pooled metric are
$$
\bar m_{c,k} = \frac{1}{32}\sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}_c} m_{b,k}, \qquad
\bar m = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{c=1}^{5}\sum_{k=1}^{10}\bar m_{c,k},
$$
where $\bar m$ equals the mean of the metric over the 160 scenarios, and
$$
\text{SE}(\bar m) = \frac{s(\{\bar m_{c,k}\})}{\sqrt{50}},
$$
with $s$ taken over the 50 values $\bar m_{c,k}$. These are the standard errors in Table \ref{tab:performance}. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ adjacent in the mean-MSE order (Design performance under queen contiguity), let $D_{c,k} = \bar m_{d,c,k} - \bar m_{d',c,k}$ for $m = \text{MSE}$. The interval for the mean difference is $\bar D \pm t_{0.975,\,49}\, s(\{D_{c,k}\})/\sqrt{50}$, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the normal approximation, is applied to the 50 values $D_{c,k}$.

## A3. Supplementary statistical comparisons

\applabel{A3}{app:supp-comparisons}This section gives the pairwise test results and two figures behind results stated in the body of this chapter.

**Pairwise tests under queen contiguity.** The four pairs that Nemenyi comparisons did not separate were $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer ($p = 0.090$), High Incidence Focus ($p = 0.130$), and Checkerboard ($p = 0.170$), and Checkerboard against High Incidence Focus ($p = 1.00$). Over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units, the mean paired differences in MSE between designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order, with $t_{49}$ 95\% intervals, were $-0.0401$ ($-0.0431$, $-0.0372$) for Incidence-Guided Saturation against Balanced Quartiles, $-0.0293$ ($-0.0332$, $-0.0255$) for Balanced Quartiles against Isolation Buffer, $-0.0853$ ($-0.0954$, $-0.0752$) for Isolation Buffer against High Incidence Focus, $-0.0738$ ($-0.0858$, $-0.0617$) for High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking, and $-0.7677$ ($-0.7893$, $-0.7460$) for $2\times2$ Blocking against Checkerboard, with Wilcoxon $p \le 4.9\times10^{-9}$ in every case. The better design of each pair had the lower MSE in all 50 units, except High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking, where it did so in 48 (96\%). This test follows the mean-MSE order. It separated High Incidence Focus from $2\times2$ Blocking, which the Nemenyi comparison of within-block ranks did not, because each unit's MSE averages over both spillover regimes, and there the control-only losses of $2\times2$ Blocking outweigh its both-arms wins.

**Pairwise tests under rook contiguity.** Nemenyi comparisons separated 13 of 15 pairs; the two they did not separate were Incidence-Guided Saturation against Balanced Quartiles ($p = 0.74$) and $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer ($p = 1.00$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer. In the surface-level comparison, Incidence-Guided Saturation had a lower MSE than Balanced Quartiles in 48 of the 50 units (mean difference $-0.0121$; $-0.0139$, $-0.0102$; Wilcoxon $p = 9.9\times10^{-10}$). $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer were close: $2\times2$ Blocking had the lower MSE in 36 of the 50 units (72\%; mean difference $-0.0048$; $-0.0078$, $-0.0017$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.0027$), but Isolation Buffer had the slightly better average rank (3.38 against 3.40), and the two designs traded places at some values of $\tau$. Every other adjacent pair differed in all 50 units. Within single incidence configurations, rook coverage was between 0.935 and 0.946 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was between 0.14 and 0.15.
