## A7. Technical notes

\applabel{A7}{app:technical}

\applabel{A7}{app:technical-notes}This section explains two results reported in the body of this chapter, the growth with $\tau$ of the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation and the rise with $\tau$ of the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity, and closes with block-level detail for the results across $\tau$. The stored results keep neither $\hat\rho$ nor the standard error of each fit, so we re-ran every block for the six designs, both neighbor types, and all five values of $\tau$, 2.4 million fits of the oracle model, recording $\hat\rho$ and the standard error, and the re-run reproduced the stored results in all 9,600 scenarios. Numbers below that involve $\hat\rho$, the standard error, or the terms of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} come from this re-run; the others come from the stored results.

### Identification diagnostics

Two combinations of design and neighbor type weaken or remove the information that separates $\tau$ from the spillover term. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard gives $WZ = 1 - Z$ exactly, because every neighbor of a treated cluster is a control and every neighbor of a control is treated. Both spillover covariates then equal $\gamma(1 - Z)$, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, so $\tau$ is not identified: the fitting routine drops the aliased spillover column, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$. Chapter 2 noted the same consequence of exact collinearity between treatment and spillover exposure, $\hat\beta \approx \beta - \psi$ in its notation. The non-oracle model has no spillover column to drop, but its Checkerboard estimates under rook contiguity have the same defect. Under queen contiguity, each of the 64 interior clusters has four treated and four control neighbors, so $WZ = 1/2$ at every interior cluster. Under the control-only regime the spillover covariate then equals $(\gamma/2)(1 - Z)$ at those clusters, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, and only the 36 clusters on the grid boundary carry information that separates it from the intercept and $Z$; $\tau$ is identified, but imprecisely. Under the both-arms regime it is the constant $\gamma/2$ at interior clusters, confounded with the intercept but not with $Z$. Isolation Buffer under rook contiguity can also, rarely, draw exactly the checkerboard pattern, a maximal independent set that equals one color class of the grid. This happened in 4 of its 40,000 rook draws and affected one fit in each of 20 scenarios, 4 at each value of $\tau$. We flag every fit in which the fitting routine reports an aliased column and every scenario in which some draw has $\text{rank}([1, Z, WZ]) < 3$. Aliased estimates are kept in all summaries. In the exhibits, we flag Checkerboard under rook contiguity, where every fit is aliased; the Isolation Buffer scenarios, each with one aliased fit among its 250, are noted here and carry no flag in the exhibits.


### Estimation error and its dependence on $\tau$

For one fit $(k, j)$, write $Y$, $Z$, and $\epsilon$ for $Y_{kj}$, $Z_{kj}$, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ (Simulation design, resampling, and metrics). Let $V = [1, Z, S(Z), X_k]$ be the $100 \times 4$ covariate matrix of the oracle model, so that Equation \ref{eq:outcome} reads $(I - \rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon$ with $\theta = (0, \tau, 1, \beta)^\top$. Let $A = (I - \rho W)^{-1}$ and $V^{+} = (V^\top V)^{-1}V^\top$, and for a vector $v$ write $[V^{+}v]_Z$ for the coefficient on $Z$ when $v$ is regressed on the columns of $V$ by least squares. Given $\hat\rho$, the estimated coefficients are $V^{+}(I - \hat\rho W)Y$ (Estimation). Because $(I - \hat\rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon + (\rho - \hat\rho)WY$ and $WY = WA(V\theta + \epsilon)$,
\begin{equation}
\hat\tau - \tau = [V^{+}\epsilon]_Z + (\rho - \hat\rho)\,h + \tau(\rho - \hat\rho)\,g,
\label{eq:error-decomposition}
\end{equation}
where
$$
g = [V^{+}WAZ]_Z, \qquad h = [V^{+}WA\{S(Z) + \beta X_k + \epsilon\}]_Z.
$$
The first term has mean zero given $Z$ and $X_k$. The last term carries a factor of $\tau$. It is present exactly when $g \neq 0$, where $g$ is the coefficient on $Z$ when the lagged treatment $WAZ = WZ + \rho W^2 Z + \rho^2 W^3 Z + \cdots$ is regressed on the model's own covariates, and its sign and size are set by the error in $\hat\rho$. The concentrated likelihood depends on $Y$ only through the residual sum of squares of $(I - \tilde\rho W)Y$ on $V$, and the part of that residual that involves $\tau$ is $\tau(\rho - \tilde\rho)$ times the residual of $WAZ$ on $V$. If $WAZ$ lies in the column space of $V$, that part vanishes for every $\tilde\rho$, so $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$; if in addition $g = 0$, then $\hat\tau - \tau$ is the same at every value of $\tau$. Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} held on every re-run fit, with a largest residual of $4.2\times10^{-13}$; for Checkerboard under rook contiguity it held in the reduced form given below.

Two consequences of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} explain the results for $\tau$ reported in the body.

First, for designs whose treated clusters have treated neighbors, the last term gives a small positive bias that grows with $\tau$. Under queen contiguity, pooled over the 160 blocks, the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.029 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.047 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.002 and 0.004. Almost all of the rise is the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition}. In our fits, $\hat\rho$ was biased downward by about 0.06 on average (for Incidence-Guided Saturation, by 0.071 at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.054 at $\tau = 3$). We observed this downward bias in these simulations; we did not derive it or check it against a published finite-sample result. With $\rho - \hat\rho$ positive on average, the last term is positive and grows with $\tau$ for any design with $g > 0$. For Incidence-Guided Saturation, $g$ averaged 0.371 over the queen fits, and the last term contributed 0.021 of the bias at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.043 at $\tau = 3$; the first term contributed 0.001 at both values, and the second 0.007 and 0.002. For Isolation Buffer, $g$ averaged 0.020, and the last term contributed 0.001 and 0.004. Most of the difference in $g$ comes from the control-only regime. Under the both-arms regime with $\rho = 0$, the lagged treatment is $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma$, one of the covariates, so $g = 0$ for every design. Under the control-only regime, $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma + Z \circ WZ$, and at $\rho = 0$, $g$ is close to the average share of treated neighbors among treated clusters. That share is 0.57 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, whose treated clusters are concentrated in the high-saturation quadrants, and exactly 0 for Isolation Buffer, whose treated clusters have no treated neighbors. For Isolation Buffer, $Z \circ WZ = 0$, so the two regimes define the same spillover covariate and the same $g$, which is 0 at $\rho = 0$ and about 0.06 at $\rho = 0.5$; at $\rho = 0$, its $\hat\rho$ and its estimation error were the same at every value of $\tau$, up to the optimizer's tolerance.

The same term explains why the control-only MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.131 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\tau = 3$ while that of Isolation Buffer did not. Under that regime, averaged over the 80 queen blocks, the variance of the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} rose from 0.008 to 0.061 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, while the variance of the rest of the error changed little (0.119 and 0.115). The variance of the last term grew more slowly than $\tau^2$ because $\hat\rho$ became less variable as $\tau$ grew. For Isolation Buffer, the variance of the last term stayed below 0.0002. The rise in bias slowed at larger values of $\tau$ for a related reason: the part of the likelihood that involves $\tau$ sharpens it around the true $\rho$ as $\tau$ grows, so the downward bias of $\hat\rho$ shrank.

Second, the decomposition explains why the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity rose with $\tau$. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard's coverage rose from 0.138 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.442 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), although its coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$ at every value of $\tau$. For this design $WZ = 1 - Z$, and because $W$ is row-standardized, $W^2 Z = W(1 - Z) = Z$. The powers of $W$ applied to $Z$ therefore alternate between $1 - Z$ and $Z$, and $WAZ = \{(1 - Z) + \rho Z\}/(1 - \rho^2)$ lies in the span of the intercept and $Z$. The derivation of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} applies with the aliased spillover column dropped, $V = [1, Z, X_k]$ and $\theta = (\gamma, \tau - \gamma, \beta)^\top$, so that $\tau - \gamma$ takes the place of $\tau$, and $g = -1/(1 + \rho)$. Two consequences follow: $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$, and
$$
\hat\tau - \tau = -\gamma + \delta + (\tau - \gamma)\,\frac{\hat\rho - \rho}{1 + \rho},
$$
where $\delta$ collects the first two terms of that decomposition and, like $\hat\rho$, does not depend on $\tau$. The error in $\hat\rho$ is therefore multiplied by $\tau - \gamma$, which grows with $\tau$. The mean standard deviation of $\hat\tau$ rose from 0.202 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.327 at $\tau = 3$, and the standard error tracked it, rising on average from 0.199 to 0.322. With the bias held near $-\gamma$, wider intervals covered $\tau$ more often. The rise was largest at $\rho = 0$ (coverage 0.145 to 0.541) and smallest at $\rho = 0.5$ (0.130 to 0.265), consistent with the factor $1/(1 + \rho)$. The same term raised the MSE from 0.477 to 0.567. About three quarters of that increase was variance, $(n-1)\text{SD}^2/n$ averaged over scenarios (Appendix \ref{app:mechanics}), which rose from 0.041 to 0.109. The other quarter was squared bias, which rose from 0.436 to 0.458 because $\hat\rho$ was biased slightly downward, moving the mean bias from $-0.650$ to $-0.667$. The higher coverage at large $\tau$ reflects wider intervals around the wrong quantity, not a recovery of $\tau$.

**Block-level detail.** Under queen contiguity, the average rank of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 1.41 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 1.85 at $\tau = 3$, while that of Balanced Quartiles stayed between 2.13 and 2.14 and that of Isolation Buffer fell from 3.71 to 3.31. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lower MSE of it and Balanced Quartiles in 103, 102, 102, 102, and 101 of the 160 blocks at $\tau = 0.8$, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3, and a lower MSE than Isolation Buffer in 75, 73, 56, 40, and 12 of the 80 control-only blocks. Its worst case across blocks was the lowest of the six designs at $\tau \le 1.5$, but at $\tau = 2$ and $\tau = 3$ that of Isolation Buffer was lower (0.207 against 0.210, and 0.208 against 0.238). Under rook contiguity, at $\tau = 3$, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lower MSE in 47 of the 80 control-only blocks, and its worst case across rook blocks was the lowest of the six designs at every value of $\tau$ except $\tau = 3$, where that of Isolation Buffer was lower (0.173 against 0.174). The coverage of rook Checkerboard was 0.138, 0.150, 0.198, 0.269, and 0.442 at $\tau = 0.8$, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3.

## A8. Observed-incidence application detail

\applabel{A8}{app:nc}The primary application numbers come from the aggregate performance and allocation-risk summaries of the main run and of the separate tail refinement. Annual tables average the six queen parameter pairs equally, without pooled Monte Carlo intervals. Each random draw used a fixed, reproducible seed. An independent check recomputed performance from the stored fits, checked annual treatment budgets and regional orderings, and checked the allocations and outcomes reused from the main run in the tail refinement. The county death-certificate source data are restricted and not publicly available; only 58-cluster summaries are reported.

For randomized designs, the prespecified refinement schedule allowed $J=100,200,400$ and $R=100,200,400,1000,2000,4000$; whichever source of Monte Carlo error, allocations or outcomes, contributed more to the shortfall from the precision targets was extended. All randomized designs met the targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$. For designs with a single possible assignment, only outcomes were extended. If an allocation occurs $n_a$ times among $J$ draws, its risk estimate enters the mean with weight $n_a/J$. The variance due to outcome noise therefore involves squared weights $(n_a/J)^2$, not $n_a/J^2$ as if duplicate estimates were independent. Bias and coverage use the same accounting of frequencies and covariances. The overall precision includes both variation across assignments and outcome noise given an assignment; a design whose sampled assignments happened to coincide is distinguished from one with only one possible assignment. Approximate Monte Carlo standard errors of setting-specific differences between designs treat the designs' random draws as independent, whereas averages across settings or models do not assume that shared allocations are independent. Settings with the same set of possible assignments shared their simulations, with annual treatment counts and population shares recalculated.

Estimated risk variance is reported raw and with its outcome Monte Carlo noise contribution subtracted. Signed corrected estimates are retained rather than silently truncated; none is negative in the NC refinement. Quantiles and worst-decile means use noisy estimated conditional risks. To avoid selection bias, worst-decile assignments were identified with one half of the simulated outcomes and evaluated with the other half, and the roles of the two halves were then reversed. The Jaccard overlap of the two worst deciles describes sampled tail membership, not a confidence interval or population tail probability. For a design with only one possible assignment, an overlap of one is uninformative.

**Design adaptations.** Before simulation, we checked the 58-cluster row-standardized contiguity matrix $W$, its binary adjacency and its row order against the boundary geometry. On the NC map, Checkerboard visits clusters by decreasing degree, chooses the arm that conflicts least with assigned neighbors, breaks equal conflicts toward control, and complements the assignment if more than half are treated. In Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves, odd-size strata receive their necessary extra treatments at random; in Balanced Halves, one half receives 14 treatments and the other 15, with the extra-treatment half chosen randomly. The four-region partition used by both saturation designs was selected from 250 candidates generated by a geographic $k$-means procedure, by compactness and balance in reference population, cluster count and county count, without consulting outcomes; reference population is pooled person-years divided by four. Incidence-Guided Saturation first ranks clusters by annual per-capita rates, averages their ranks equally within each region, ranks those four means, and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest. Regional ties are broken randomly per allocation, and local treatment counts are rounded under the retained design rules. Per-capita cluster rates already account for population size; regional mean ranks answer an equally weighted cluster question, whereas pooled regional deaths/population weights larger clusters more heavily. Mean raw rates and pooled regional rates are evaluated as prespecified sensitivities rather than chosen by performance. The grid rule averages $X$ directly: mean ranks align with its rank-scaled Poisson cases but are a deliberate adaptation for the application, rather than the exact rule used for continuous grid incidence. The 14 groups used by $2\times2$ Blocking are formed once per year by $k$-means on standardized projected coordinates, incidence ranks and log(1+population), then held fixed; half of each group, rounded, is treated at random, and the single-cluster group of each year remains control, because half of one cluster rounds to zero. This is not a set of literal square blocks.

The fixed regional criterion is $C=3s_P+1.5s_K+1.5s_D+c/d_{\max}$, where $s_P$, $s_K$ and $s_D$ are the standard deviations of regional population, cluster and county shares. Here $c$ averages within-region distances to regional centers and $d_{\max}$ is the maximum pairwise distance between the projected cluster coordinates. Candidates use standardized projected coordinates and are selected without outcome performance. The fixed groups used by $2\times2$ Blocking contain one to eight clusters; yearly total treatments are 28, 31, 27 and 29. Table \ref{tab:nc-order} documents alternative summaries before performance evaluation.
